title: King v. Burwell (2015)
summary: The Affordable Care Act makes premium tax credits available on federally run exchanges as well as state-run ones, and the Court decided that question itself rather than deferring to the IRS.
notes:
Key line: "Congress passed the Affordable Care Act to improve health insurance markets, not to destroy them." Chief Justice Roberts, for the Court.

Citation: 576 U.S. 473 (2015).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were David King and three other Virginia residents who did not want to buy health insurance. Virginia had declined to set up its own exchange, so its residents used the federal exchange. Respondents were Sylvia Burwell, Secretary of Health and Human Services, and other federal officials responsible for administering the Affordable Care Act and the Internal Revenue Code. The petitioners argued that if tax credits were unavailable on the federal exchange, insurance would cost them more than eight percent of income and they would be exempt from the coverage requirement. The Government defended the IRS rule making credits available in every state.
sections.Material Facts: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010 combined guaranteed issue and community rating rules, a requirement that individuals maintain coverage or make a payment, and tax credits for people with household incomes between 100 and 400 percent of the poverty line. Section 36B of the Internal Revenue Code computes the credit by reference to insurance bought through an Exchange established by the State under section 18031. Section 18041 directs the Secretary of HHS to establish such Exchange in a state that does not create its own. The IRS adopted a rule in 2012 providing that credits are available regardless of whether the exchange is state or federal. Sixteen states plus the District of Columbia ran their own exchanges; the remaining 34 states used a federal exchange.
sections.Procedural History: The petitioners sued in the Eastern District of Virginia, challenging the IRS rule. The District Court dismissed the suit, holding that the Act unambiguously made credits available on federal exchanges. The Fourth Circuit affirmed in 2014 but found the statute ambiguous and deferred to the IRS under Chevron. The same day, a D.C. Circuit panel reached the opposite conclusion in Halbig v. Burwell. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in November 2014 and affirmed the Fourth Circuit on June 25, 2015.
sections.Issue: Section 36B of the Internal Revenue Code ties the premium tax credit to insurance bought through an Exchange established by the State under section 18031, while section 18041 directs the Secretary of HHS to establish such Exchange in states that decline to create one. Thirty-four states used a federal exchange. Are the Affordable Care Act's premium tax credits available to individuals who buy insurance through an exchange established by the federal government, and should a court answer that question under Chevron deference to the IRS or by determining the best reading of the statute itself?
sections.Holding: Yes. Read in context and in light of the Act's structure, the phrase an Exchange established by the State under section 18031 includes an exchange that HHS establishes in a state's place. Congress made credits available in every state so that the guaranteed issue and community rating reforms would work. The Court declined to apply Chevron because the question was one of deep economic and political significance that Congress would not have delegated to the IRS. The Fourth Circuit's judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts first explained why Chevron did not govern. The availability of billions of dollars in credits affecting millions of people is central to the statutory scheme; had Congress wished to assign that question to an agency, it would have done so expressly, and not to the IRS, which has no expertise in health policy. The Court therefore had to decide the correct reading. The phrase established by the State, read in isolation, seemed to favor the petitioners, but the Court found it ambiguous in context. Section 18041 tells the Secretary to establish such Exchange, which points back to the state exchange under section 18031, suggesting the two are equivalent. Other provisions would make no sense if federal exchanges lacked qualified individuals, and the Act elsewhere assumes that credits are available in every state. The Court then turned to structure. Without credits, the coverage requirement would exempt most people in federal-exchange states while guaranteed issue and community rating remained, producing the adverse selection death spiral that Congress designed the Act to prevent. Congress passed the Act to improve insurance markets, not to destroy them. The Court acknowledged that the Act was drafted behind closed doors and through reconciliation, producing inartful language, but held that the legislative plan controlled.

topics.lrs-i-major-questions: King withholds deference on a major question while independently accepting the agency’s construction.
topics.lrs-i-historical-chevron: King is an exception to the historical Chevron allocation of interpretive authority.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: The majority read 'Exchange established by the State' in light of the ACA's interlocking provisions rather than in isolation.
topics.lrs-i-independent-judgment: Loper Bright cites King as an example of a court deciding statutory meaning itself instead of deferring, so it previews the post-Chevron approach.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3. Justice Scalia dissented, joined by Justices Thomas and Alito. He argued that established by the State plainly excludes the federal government, that the Act uses the phrase deliberately in many places, that Congress may have wanted to pressure states into building exchanges, and that the majority rewrote the statute to save it, remarking that the law should be called SCOTUScare.
